texts: good. salt-bloom keeps its bloom genus and takes crust as its kind, with "pale" and "crystalline" recorded as separate properties rather than fused into the kind name.

bad: the sentence states a standing fact, but it is stored as one particular growing event with the word "salt-bloom" sitting in a participant slot, so nothing is claimed about any actual salt-bloom; on top of that "submerged tide-pool stones" forces into existence one specific set of submerged stones the general claim never introduced. Putting the condition in its own finite clause fixes both: "When a tide-pool stone is submerged, salt-bloom grows on it."

bad: as with the growing sentence, the claim is stored as a single smelling event with "salt-bloom" in a participant slot instead of as a general fact, and the frame is awkward for us besides - in "X smells of Y" there is no settled role for the thing giving off the smell, and "faintly" has no settled slot either. Recasting it as a property of countable crusts avoids all three: "Salt-bloom crusts have a faint smell of salt."
good. it becomes a standing rule over Keepers, with salt-bloom as what is harvested and each Keeper's own wooden scraper as the tool; the scraper keeps both its scraper genus and its wooden property.

mixed: the causing frame is recorded correctly (iron does it, the crumbling is what it brings about), but salt-bloom is filed as the doer of the crumbling rather than as the thing that crumbles, and the claim is stored as one incident rather than a standing truth. The wording is not really at fault - that doer slip is ours to fix on the next parse - but if you want to sidestep the make-something-happen frame that caused it, write "Iron crumbles salt-bloom."

mixed: the parse was judged faithful and the packets, the salt-bloom and the Cauldron Hall store are all recorded, but the bare plural subject turns this into a claim about waxed paper packets in general - every such packet anywhere holds this salt-bloom in that store - when what you are saying is where the salt-bloom is kept. Making the salt-bloom the subject keeps the meaning and drops the over-broad reading: "The salt-bloom is kept in waxed paper packets in the Cauldron Hall store."
good. a standing rule over Keepers, with salt-bloom as what is added, mire-essence as what it goes into, and winter recorded as the time.

bad: the claim is stored as one particular slowing event with "salt-bloom" itself in the doer slot and at full single-fact confidence, so it neither reaches any actual salt-bloom nor reads as a general truth, and "the burn" pins it to one particular burning of mire-essence. Giving the subject a countable plural fixes the half the wording controls: "Salt-bloom crusts slow the burn of mire-essence." (the definite "the burn" is ours to sort out).
